casualties.title: Wheelchair user, chair wrecked, otherwise well
casualties.approach: Man sitting on the footpath with dust on his clothes, calm, with his wheelchair wrecked and tipped on its side beside him, saying he is not hurt.

params.text: I'm not hurt. My chair's wrecked.

history.mechanism: He was tipped out of his wheelchair onto the footpath when the earthquake hit, and a falling shop sign crushed the chair. He pulled himself clear and is not hurt.
history.background: Paraplegia from a spinal injury 15 years ago; uses a manual wheelchair every day and has no feeling below the waist.

deterioration.note: Left on the cold ground for a long time. He is chilled and uncomfortable, and he cannot feel pressure building under him. Vitals are unchanged, so he is still orange.

params.text: I've been on cold ground a while now.

teaching: Not being able to walk because of a disability is not an injury, but he cannot reach the walking-wounded point, so the placeholder sieve tags him orange (NZRT to confirm).
Ask how he usually gets around and what he needs; he knows his body and his equipment better than you do.
Never lift or drag him without asking how he wants to be moved.
Keep his chair or its parts with him so the next team can use them, and tell them he should not sit on cold ground for long.

casualties.title: Wheelchair user who can get to the collection point
casualties.approach: Woman sitting in her wheelchair at the roadside, calm, with grazes on both palms, saying she can get herself to the point.

params.text: I can get myself to the point.

history.mechanism: Left her flat in the tsunami warning and pushed her wheelchair up the hill road over fallen branches and gravel. She grazed both palms on the wheels.
history.background: Spina bifida; uses a manual wheelchair full time.

findings.label: Grazed left palm from pushing the wheel
Grazed right palm from pushing the wheel

teaching: A wheelchair user who can get herself to the collection point is walking wounded under the placeholder rules, so she is green (NZRT to confirm).
Ask what she can do, such as getting herself to the point, instead of telling her to stand up and walk.
Her hands are how she moves, so tell the walking-wounded team to look at the grazes early.
Offer help over rough ground, but ask before you take hold of her chair.

casualties.title: Shaky walker with type 1 diabetes, sugar early
casualties.approach: Woman standing in wet clothes at the evacuation point, shaking, pale and sweating, looking distressed and saying she is fine, just shaky.

params.text: I'm fine, stop fussing. Just shaky.

history.mechanism: Evacuated from the flooded streets at midday and held at the crossing for hours. She took her insulin this morning but has not eaten since breakfast.

deterioration.note: Blood sugar keeps falling. She becomes confused, sits down, cannot stand and stops following commands.
She becomes drowsy and now responds only to voice. She is no longer talking sensibly.

teaching: Shaky, pale and sweaty while still walking and talking can be low blood sugar, not just cold, so ask if she has diabetes.
Give sugar by mouth early, and only while she is awake, following commands and able to swallow safely.
Once she is confused or drowsy she is red, and nothing goes by mouth because it can enter the airway.
Low blood sugar can look like a head injury or being drunk, so think of it in any confused casualty.

casualties.title: Severe asthma in a dusty evacuation hall, own inhaler
casualties.approach: Teenage boy sitting on the floor of a dusty school hall, one hand on his chest, sweating and speaking only a few words at a time, saying his puffer is in his pocket.

history.mechanism: Ceiling tiles fell in the school hall during the earthquake. Dust and fright set off a severe asthma attack; he is too breathless to get his reliever out.
history.medications: Blue salbutamol reliever inhaler (in his jacket pocket) and a daily preventer
history.background: Asthma since primary school; admitted to hospital once

deterioration.note: Exhaustion. His breathing rate falls to 8 or 9 and his chest goes quiet. He is drowsy, responds only to voice and no longer follows commands. This is worse, not better.
He tires completely and stops breathing. There is no breathing after the airway is opened.

teaching: Speaking only a few words at a time and breathing over 30 a minute is a severe asthma attack, so he is red.
Help him use his own reliever straight away; it takes seconds and can stop the attack getting worse.
In severe asthma a breathing rate that falls to 8 or 9 with a quiet chest and drowsiness means exhaustion, so keep him red and re-check rather than down-triage.
Check severe asthma casualties again soon, because a tired casualty can stop breathing quickly.
